author: high3
claim: For a real polynomial p, put r(x)=p(x)-x. The existence of a real polynomial q satisfying p(p(x))-x=(p(x)-x)^2q(x) is equivalent to either r=0 or r divides r'+2. Consequently p must be of the form p(x)=x+c or p(x)=-x+c.
evidence: Since p(x)=x+r(x), p(p(x))-x=r(x)+r(x+r(x)). Expanding the polynomial r at x with increment r(x) gives r(x+r(x))=r(x)+r(x)r'(x)+r(x)^2S(x) for some S in R[x]. Thus p(p(x))-x=r(x)(2+r'(x))+r(x)^2S(x). For nonzero r, divisibility by r^2 is equivalent to r dividing 2+r'. If deg r>=2 this is impossible since deg(2+r')<deg r. If deg r=1, it forces r'=-2, giving p=-x+c. If deg r=0 it gives p=x+c, including r=0. Conversely p=x+c works with q=2/c for c nonzero (and q=0 for c=0), while p=-x+c works with q=0.

links.statement: The equation is equivalent to a first-derivative divisibility condition and its solutions are exactly translations and affine involutions.

glossary.S: the real polynomial arising from the exact Taylor expansion of r(x+r(x)) beyond the constant and linear terms

author: high2
claim: The target condition is equivalent, after setting f(x)=p(x)-x, to f(x)^2 dividing f(x)+f(x+f(x)); every nonzero f satisfying it obeys f(x) divides 2+f'(x). Consequently f is constant or f'(x)=-2, so the only candidates are p(x)=x+c and p(x)=-x+c.
evidence: Write p(y)=y+f(y). Then p(p(x))-x=f(x)+f(x+f(x)). For n=deg f, the exact finite Taylor identity gives f(x+f(x))=f(x)+f'(x)f(x)+f(x)^2 H(x), where H is a real polynomial (the sum of terms of Taylor order at least 2). Hence f(x)+f(x+f(x))=f(x)(2+f'(x))+f(x)^2H(x). If nonzero f has its square dividing this expression, cancellation in R[x] gives f | 2+f'. If f is nonconstant of degree n, then 2+f' is either zero or has degree at most n-1, so divisibility forces 2+f'=0 and f=-2x+c. Constant f gives p=x+c. Direct substitution shows both families work.

links.statement: The classification mechanism for the full target.

glossary.H: The real polynomial collecting the Taylor terms of order at least two.
glossary.n: The degree of the nonzero polynomial f.

author: xhigh
claim: For a nonidentity real polynomial p, the existence of q with p(p(x))-x=(p(x)-x)^2q(x) is equivalent to p(x)-x dividing p'(x)+1 in R[x].
evidence: Set r(x)=p(x)-x. For a polynomial p there is S(x,y) in R[x,y] with p(x+y)=p(x)+y p'(x)+y^2S(x,y), by expanding each monomial. Substitution y=r(x) gives p(p(x))-x=r(x)(1+p'(x))+r(x)^2S(x,r(x)). If r is nonzero, equality with r^2q is equivalent, after cancellation in the integral domain R[x], to r dividing 1+p'. Conversely that divisibility inserted in the displayed expansion constructs a polynomial q.

links.statement: equivalence of composition divisibility and derivative divisibility

glossary.q: a real polynomial witnessing the required identity
glossary.S: a real bivariate polynomial giving the exact first-order expansion of p

author: xhigh
claim: Any nonidentity solution p has degree at most one.
evidence: By the established-in-this-finding derivation, p-x divides p'+1. If deg p=n>=2, then deg(p-x)=n and deg(p'+1)=n-1, with p'+1 nonzero, contradicting the elementary degree inequality for nonzero polynomial divisibility. Therefore deg p<=1.

author: xhigh
claim: The complete candidate classification is p(x)=x+c or p(x)=-x+c for an arbitrary real constant c.
evidence: Write p(x)=ax+b. If p is not the identity, divisibility p-x | p'+1 says ((a-1)x+b) divides a+1. If a=1 this gives all nonidentity translations (b nonzero), and the identity is separately valid. If a is not 1, the divisor is linear, so the constant dividend must vanish: a+1=0. Hence a=-1 and b is arbitrary. Direct substitution gives q=2/c for p=x+c with c nonzero, q=0 for p=x, and q=0 for p=-x+c.

glossary.q: a real polynomial witnessing the identity
glossary.a: the coefficient of x in the affine expression for p
glossary.b: the constant term in the affine expression for p

author: xhigh4
claim: For real polynomials p and q, set r(x)=p(x)-x. If r is nonzero, the identity p(p(x))-x=r(x)^2q(x) holds if and only if r(x) divides r'(x)+2 in R[x].
evidence: Since p(x)=x+r(x), one has p(p(x))-x=r(x+r(x))+r(x). Writing r(t)=sum_{k=0}^d a_k t^k and expanding each (x+r(x))^k by the binomial theorem yields a polynomial S with r(x+r(x))=r(x)+r'(x)r(x)+r(x)^2S(x). Hence p(p(x))-x=r(x)(r'(x)+2)+r(x)^2S(x). If the target identity holds, cancellation in the integral domain R[x] gives r'(x)+2=r(x)(q(x)-S(x)); conversely this divisibility lets one choose q=S+(r'+2)/r.

links.statement: The original identity is equivalent, for nonzero r, to r | (r'+2).

glossary.S: A real polynomial collecting all Taylor/binomial terms of order at least two in r(x).

author: xhigh4
claim: The only possible real polynomials p in the problem are p(x)=x+c or p(x)=-x+c, where c is real, and every such polynomial works.
evidence: Use r=p-id. The zero polynomial r gives p=x. If r is a nonzero constant c, then p=x+c. If deg r=d>0 and r divides r'+2, either r'+2=0 or its degree is strictly less than d; a nonzero polynomial of smaller degree cannot be divisible by r, so r'+2=0. Thus r=-2x+c and p=-x+c. Conversely, if p=x+c with c nonzero, choose q=2/c; if c=0 both sides vanish (choose q=0); if p=-x+c then p(p(x))=x and q=0 works.

glossary.d: The positive degree of r in the nonconstant case.
